abstract:  "Cementitious ground support systems, such as shotcrete, cast-in-place linings, cemented backfill, and grouted bolts, are essential for excavation stability in deep underground mines facing high stresses, seismicity, and harsh groundwater conditions. This paper reviews sensing technologies for these systems using a lifecycle framework spanning five phases: (1) placement and early-age, (2) early service, (3) long-term degradation, (4) dynamic events, and (5) post-event assessment. For each phase, key physical variables (temperature, maturity, strain,stress, corrosion, creep, dynamic response, geometric change) are mapped to appropriate sensing methods: thermal, maturity monitoring, mechanical,deformation sensing, wave-based damage detection, durability/chemical measurements, and geometric mapping. System integration aspects—underground communication, data fusion, AI/ML predictive models, and digital twins—are discussed, alongside challenges in sensor robustness, standardization/QAQC, data management, and transitioning to risk-informed control. The review identifies priorities for future research to enable reliable, lifecycle-oriented monitoring that enhances safety and productivity in underground mining."

# Introduction

## Background and motivation

As underground mines extend to greater depths, they are increasingly exposed to high in situ stresses, high temperatures, and more complex hydrogeological conditions [@ref-deep-mining; @ref-high-stress-mines]. Under these conditions, the stability of excavations depends critically on the performance of ground support systems, which must accommodate both static ground loads and dynamic events such as blasting and rockbursts [@ref-ground-support; @ref-rockburst]. Cementitious materials, including shotcrete, cast‑in‑place linings, cemented backfill, and grouted bolts, which form a major component of this support system because they can be adapted to irregular geometries, provide good load re-equilibrium, and are relatively cost‑effective [@ref-shotcrete-review; @ref-backfill-review].

However, the performance of cementitious support is strongly time‑dependent and environment‑sensitive. Its performance evolves from fresh slurry through early‑age strength gain to long term service, and the degradation occurs by creep, shrinkage, cracking, corrosion, and chemical attack over time[@ref-taheri; @ref-time-dependent-concrete]. In deep, high‑stress mines, these processes are further coupled with stress redistribution, seismic loading, and groundwater inflow, making it difficult to verify design assumptions using traditional visual inspection and spot measurements alone [@ref-deep-mine-concrete]. This motivates the use of dedicated sensing technologies to provide quantitative information on the state and evolution of cementitious support in situ.

## Importance of ground support and monitoring

Throughout the lifecycle of cementitious support, from placement to end of service, different physical processes control safety and serviceability.[@ref-shm-concrete] At early ages, temperature evolution, moisture condition, setting time, and strength gain govern re‑entry decisions and quality control for shotcrete, linings, and backfill [@ref-maturity-mining; @ref-shotcrete-monitoring]. In service, structural response becomes dominant: stress and strain in shotcrete and grouted bolts, cracking and debonding at the rock–support interface,  and the onset of time‑dependent deformation [@ref-ground-support-interaction]. Over longer time scales, durability issues such as corrosion of reinforcement, carbonation, leaching, and sulphate attack reduce residual capacity and can lead to costly rehabilitation or unplanned downtime [@ref-durability-mining; @ref-corrosion-concrete].

Sensing technologies provide a means to track these processes quantitatively and to connect them with operational decisions. Various sensors can supply information on temperature, strain, deformation, damage, and degradation that is not accessible through routine inspections alone [@ref-shm-framework]. When appropriately integrated with mine communication systems and data analytics, such monitoring can support safer re‑entry criteria, more targeted reinforcement, optimized backfilling and extraction sequences, and earlier detection of emerging hazards [@ref-mining-monitoring; @ref-risk-based-mining].

## Scope and structure of the review

Cementitious materials are used in several key support functions in underground mining, including shotcrete linings in drifts and intersections, cast‑in‑place and precast shaft linings, cemented paste or rockfill in stopes, and cementitious grout around bolts and cables [@ref-shotcrete-review; @ref-backfill-review]. This paper focuses on sensing technologies that are directly applicable to these cement‑based systems, rather than to rock mass monitoring or general mine‑wide geotechnical instrumentation.

The review is organized around a lifecycle perspective. First, the main types of cementitious ground support, their operating environments, and dominant failure mechanisms are summarized to establish monitoring needs. And then introduces a phase‑based framework that links five stages of the support lifecycle to physical variables and associated sensing targets. On this basis, sensing technologies are grouped by their primary measurement function (thermal–maturity, mechanical response, deformation, damage/wave‑based methods, durability/chemical, and geometric/global mapping) and mapped to the phases where they provide the useful parameters. Subsequent sections discuss system‑level integration, including underground communication, data fusion, AI/ML, and digital twin concepts, and finally outline current key challenges and future research directions for deploying sensing technologies in cementitious ground support systems in underground mines.

# Cementitious support types in underground mining

Concrete is one of the most widely used cementitious materials in mining, providing durable, relatively low‑cost, and versatile support for shafts, drifts, excavations, and surface infrastructure. From the moment concrete is mixed and placed until the end of its service life, multiple properties must be monitored to ensure that design strength is reached and maintained, and to optimize construction and production schedules [@taheriReviewFiveKey2019]. The relevant parameters depend on the support function, construction method, and age, and include inherent attributes (temperature, humidity, pH, thermal and electrical conductivity, hydration degree, microstructure) and induced attributes (strain, stress, cracking, corrosion, stiffness, strength, and maturity). If abnormal changes in these parameters are not detected and acted upon, ground support performance can deteriorate, leading to increased risk of instability and lost productivity.

## Shotcrete

Shotcrete is a concrete or mortar mix that is conveyed through a hose and pneumatically projected at high velocity onto rock surfaces, typically in wet‑mix or dry‑mix form. Its ability to rapidly bond to irregular rock surfaces and gain early strength makes it the dominant primary support method in many underground mines. The durability of shotcrete is influenced by electrochemical corrosion, freeze–thaw cycles, alkali–aggregate reaction, elevated temperature exposure, microbiological attack, and mechanical damage, which can lead to shrinkage cracking, debonding, and spalling [@galanDurabilityShotcreteUnderground2019].

## Operating environment and constraints

blasting vibration, water inflow, temperature gradients

sensing constraint requirements: installation time, maitainability, cost, performance test

The operating environment is not stable like a building, all devices, equipments, and even tunnels will change with the open-stop moving forward. During the mining process, explosives might be used for caving the minerals, and it can produce powerful impact wave to affect the support stability and integrity; Due to the mining system high probablity through the aquiffer, the water inflow from the aquiffer will change the support physical properties and reduce the longevity of sensors. In deep mine, the high temperature gradients might cause the extra temperature drift error on sensor. There are also some security requirements must conform, in particular the coal mine, which includes the gas, and combustiable coal dust.

Thus, these harsh environment and constraints need to have more strict requirements. high stress, dynamic  loading, and ground water erosion can degrade sensors or affect signal stability. On the another hand, because the absence of GPS, underground mining requires complex wireless signal networks to transmit data from embedded sensors.

## The lifecycle of cementitious support

In underground mining, sensing technology must ultimately support specific operational decisions rather than purely academic measurement. Key decisions include re‑entry time after shotcrete application, verification of support re-entry time, support quality(QA/QC), recovery timing, and hazard alert. Therefore, the lifecycle of cementitious support divided into five phases, each phase should be mapped to both its measurement function and the associated decision or alarm logic.

# Failure mechanisms and monitoring requirements

## Early-age risks
> Hydration heat, thermal gradients, moisture loss, setting time, strength development, shrinkage cracking

These correspond to : temperature and humiduty history, maturity and strength, thickness and coverage

Early‑age risks include excessive hydration heat, steep thermal gradients, rapid moisture loss, delayed setting, insufficient early strength, and shrinkage cracking. These phenomena are governed by the temperature and humidity history, degree of hydration, and restraint conditions. Monitoring strategies therefore emphasize embedded thermocouples and maturity sensors, humidity and moisture probes, ultrasonic or impact‑echo methods for stiffness evolution, and external tools such as LiDAR or thickness gauges to verify coverage and geometry.


## Mechnical damage and structural instability
> Flexural cracking, debonding from rock, shear, punching, layers delamination
> These correspond to: strain/stress, crack initiation and growth, adhesion, displacement and convergence

Shotcrete is a special type of  concrete that is pheumatically projected at high velocity onto a surface. Shotcrete is typically classified into wet-mix and dry-mix types,depending on the method of mixing and delivery. Shotcrete is widely used in underground mining for ground support, tunnel linings, and slope stabilization due to its versatility, rapid application, and strong bonding properties.

Recycled concrete [@liuExperimentalStudyFailure2011]

fibre reinforced concrete [@wangMechanicalPropertiesFailure2025]

## Time-dependent deformation 

Creep and shrinkage of cementitious materials and thier effects  are two main failure types, "Serviceabiliti failures of concrete structures involving excessive cracking or deflection are relatively common, even in structures that comply with code requirements." [@gilbertTimeDependentBehaviourConcrete2010;@StateArtTimedependent2013]. Another failure type is the time dependent diffusion and corrosion, which is more related to the chemical and electrochemical degradation.

For the creep and shrinkage failure, The strain is discomposed into the creep strain $\epsilon_{cr}(t)$, shrinkage strain $\epsilon_{sh}(t)$, and the instantaneous strain $\epsilon_{e}(t)$ and the temperature strain $\epsilon_{T}(t)$, which is the sum of the elastic strain $\epsilon_{e}$ and the plastic strain $\epsilon_{p}$, as :

$$
\epsilon(t) = \epsilon_{e}(t) + \epsilon_{p}(t) + \epsilon_{cr}(t) + \epsilon_{sh}(t) + \epsilon_{T}(t)
$${#eq-time-dependent-strain}

The components of the strain over time can be calculated by proper assumptions and models, @gilbert2010time gave a comprehensive analysis and calculation for @eq-time-dependent-strain.

In practice, time‑dependent deformation is tracked using embedded strain gauges, vibrating wire instruments, extensometers, and distributed fibre optic sensing, while corrosion and carbonation are monitored via half‑cell potential measurements, resistivity mapping, embedded reference electrodes, and in some cases self‑sensing cementitious composites with conductive networks.

## Corrosion and carbonization

Corrosion and carbonization are two widespread problem affecting cementitious materials, and they are also the time-dependent failure types, but they are not like the creep and shrinkage, which is more related to the mechanical deformation, but more related to the chemical and electrochemical degradation @agboolaReviewCorrosionConcrete2021. For improving the strength and durability, steel reinforcement is widely used in cast-in-place concrete, but the corrosion of steel reinforcement is more serious than the concrete itself, with costly repair in billions of dollars annually worldwide @quraishiCorrosionReinforcedSteel2017.The time-dependent reduction coefficient can be calculated by laboratory methods, and the deptth of carbonation increses over time (as shown in the @fig-carbonation),  @nokkenTimeDependentDiffusion2006 based on three methods obtaining service life of concrete structure in laboratory sucessfully.

![Schematic representation of the carbonation of concrete, adapted from @felixParametricAnalysisCarbonation2017](./assets/carbonation.png){#fig-carbonation width=70%}

The main cause of carbonnation the the gaseous $CO_2$ entering , and then diffusing and dissolution into the cementious materials through the pores and fractures. It has two major processes, the formation of carbonic acid and the neutralization rection, as shown in the @eq-carbonation-1 and @eq-carbonation-2.

$$
CO_2 + H_2O \rightarrow H_2CO_3
$${#eq-carbonation-1}

$$
H_2CO_3 + Ca(OH)_2 \rightarrow CaCO_3 + 2H_2O
$${#eq-carbonation-2}

Over time, this reaction can also affect other hydration products like Calcium Silicate Hydrate (C-S-H) gel, causing it to decalcify and further lowering the pH.

![Schematics of corrosion adapted from @goyalReviewCorrosionProtection2018](./assets/2026-03-16-15-04-20.png){#fig-corrosion width=70%}

Corrosion is often caused by the by chloride ions. Unlike carbonation, which lowers the pH of the entire concrete matrix, chloride-induced corrosion is a more aggresive and localized mechanism. The chloride ions can move through the three main processes: diffusion, capillary absorption, and permeation, enventually reaching the steel reinforcement. There are also two phases of chloride ingress: initiation phase and propagation phase.

In the initiation phase, chloride ions just penetrate the surface and accumulate in the concrete structure, in particular in the steel surface, but they don't cause corrosion in this phase, yet. Once the critical chloride threshold is reached, the propagation phase starts, and  the anodic reaction and cathodic reaction occur, the chmechical reaction of the corrosion process is shown in the @eq-corrosion-1 and @eq-corrosion-2.
$$
Fe \rightarrow Fe^{2+} + 2e^-
$${#eq-corrosion-1}
$$
2H_2O + O_2 + 4e^- \rightarrow 4OH^-
$${#eq-corrosion-2}

The @eq-corrosion-2 comsumes the electrons generated by the @eq-corrosion-1, and produces the hydroxide ions, which can further react with the ferrous ions to form the rust products, such as $Fe(OH)_2$ and $Fe(OH)_3$. The corrosion process can cause the expansion of the steel reinforcement, which can lead to cracking and spalling of the concrete cover, and eventually structural failure.

## Phase I: placement and early-age

Target: re-entry time, early-age strength, thickness/cover (QA/QC)
Key physical paramerter: temperature hydration heat, marturity/ strenth proxy, thickness/geometry, moisture

The early-age phase (0–48 h) is critical for re-entry decisions and quality control. Monitoring focuses on indirect proxies of strength development, primarily temperature evolution, moisture condition, and early stiffness. Thermocouples are widely used to record hydration temperature history, which can be converted to in-situ strength using maturity methods [@taheriReviewFiveKey2019]. Distributed temperature sensing (DTS) further enables continuous spatial monitoring but requires careful installation and cost considerations. 

Moisture sensors help assess curing conditions, while non-destructive methods such as ultrasonic pulse velocity (UPV) provide indirect evaluation of stiffness development by measuring wave propagation velocity in the material [@malhotraNondestructiveTestingConcrete2004]. In addition, LiDAR and laser scanning are increasingly used to verify shotcrete thickness and coverage at the system scale.

Overall, sensing in this phase relies on thermal–hydraulic–stiffness proxies to support re-entry time and QA/QC decisions.


## Phase II: Early service and load adaptation

target: early cracking/debonding, load redistribution, whether reinforcement is needed
key parameter: strain/stress evolution, interface behavior, crack initiation

During early service (days to weeks), the support system begins to interact with the surrounding rock mass, and monitoring shifts toward structural response. Strain gauges and vibrating wire sensors are commonly used to measure stress and strain evolution, while fibre optic sensing (FBG and distributed systems) enables spatially continuous monitoring of deformation and strain localization [@baoRecentProgressDistributed2021]. Acoustic emission techniques can detect microcrack initiation and debonding at the support–rock interface, providing early warning of damage [@grosseAcousticEmissionTesting2008].

In this phase, sensing is primarily used to detect load redistribution and early damage, supporting decisions on reinforcement and support optimization.

## Phase III: Long-term service and degradation
target: durability/ residual capacity, maintenance shceduling, failure prevention
key parameter: creep/ shrinkage, corrosion/carbonation, moisture and permeability

In the long-term stage (months to years), monitoring focuses on time-dependent deformation and durability-related processes such as creep, shrinkage, and corrosion. Extensometers, vibrating wire gauges, and distributed fibre optic sensing are used to track deformation over time, while durability is assessed through electrical resistivity, half-cell potential, and embedded electrode sensors [@agboolaReviewCorrosionConcrete2021]. Moisture and transport properties also play a key role in interpreting degradation mechanisms.

Sensing in this phase supports maintenance planning and residual capacity assessment by capturing both mechanical and chemical degradation processes.

FIX: move DFOS
Compared with traditional sonsors that only can be performed on specific points, specific time, or single parameter, distributed fibre optic sensing (DFOS) provides continuous spatial monitoring of strain and temperature, which is particularly valuable for detecting localized deformation and damage. However, its application in underground mining remains challenging due to complex geometries, installation constraints, and harsh environmental conditions, requiring careful system design and calibration.

## Phase IV: Safety events and system-level response
target: rockburst/blasting damage detectioni, rapid safety assessment, evacuation / alarm trigger
key parameter: high-frequency strain/stress, vibration wave propagation, global defformation

Dynamic loading from blasting and seismic activity introduces high strain rates and rapid damage evolution. Monitoring in this phase relies on high-frequency sensing techniques such as acoustic emission and microseismic systems to capture fracture processes and energy release [@grosseAcousticEmissionTesting2008]. In addition, rapid scanning methods such as LiDAR can be used for post-event deformation assessment.

In addition to conventional sensing systems, emerging self-sensing cementitious materials provide an alternative approach by embedding sensing capability directly into the material. The self-sensing principle has been massive studying in decades, as a novel concepts without traditional sensor achieving the monitoring function for the stress, strain, crack and flaws. Self-sensing function is obtained from the piezoresistive effect of functional fillers, which are scattered in the matrix phase and form a conductive network or planes [@bekzhanovaSelfSensingCementitiousComposites2021a]

## Phase V: Post-event assessment and rehabilitation
target: damage mapping, decision: repair, reinforce/ abandon
key parameter: geometry change, crack network, internal defects

After extreme events or during scheduled inspections, sensing focuses on damage mapping and structural assessment. LiDAR, photogrammetry, and ground penetrating radar (GPR) are commonly used to identify geometric changes, cracking, and internal defects. Non-destructive methods such as ultrasonic and impact-echo testing can further evaluate internal integrity.

This phase supports decisions on repair, reinforcement, or decommissioning of support systems.

# System integration

The transition from individual sensor measurements to actionable engineering decisions requires a robust intelligent integration framework. In the harsh environment of underground mining, system integration must address the physical challenges of signal propagation, the time sync challenges of multi-stage data fusion, and the algorithmic challenges of converting raw signals into structural health indicators.

## Underground  communication and data transmission

Underground mining has complex geometry, metallic infrastructure, and no GPS, which makes wireless communication challenging [@ref-underground-comms]. Common technologies such as Wi‑Fi, Zigbee, Bluetooth, and LoRa offer different trade‑offs between data rate, range, and power consumption; long‑range systems typically support lower data rates, whereas high‑bandwidth systems require denser infrastructure and shorter links. The relationship between data rates and transimission range is shown as the @fig-data-transer-system [@ngwenyamaRecentAdvancesChallenges2025]. For cementitious support monitoring, low‑rate measurements (temperature, humidity, strain from vibrating‑wire gauges) can use low‑power, long‑range protocols, while high‑volume data from AE, microseismic, LiDAR, or high‑rate DFOS usually require local buffering, image processing, and higher‑bandwidth backhaul, such as industrial Ethernet or mine‑wide Wi‑Fi [@ref-shm-mining].

![Comparison of wireless communication systems](assets/2026-03-12-15-45-30.png){#fig-data-transer-system width=80%}

Note: this figure provides a qualitative comparison only; actual data rates and transmission ranges vary significantly depending on environment conditions and specific protocal version.

## Multi-Modal data fusion

No single sensor can fully describe the condition of shotcrete, backfill, or grouted bolts and their environment, so practical systems combine embedded sensors with external measurements such as LiDAR, photogrammetry, and ground penetrating radar [@ref-shm-framework]. A simple three‑layer framework is often adopted: data acquisition and normalization (synchronizing and cleaning heterogeneous data), state estimation and feature extraction (e.g., maturity‑based strength, convergence rates, corrosion indices), and situation assessment (translating indicators into condition states or risk levels for drifts, panels, or shaft segments) [@ref-struct-health]. This layered approach needs amount of data analysis and building the relationships between different data sources, which helps connect detailed measurements at a few locations with lower‑frequency, large‑scale observations, and makes it easier to define consistent alarm thresholds and QA/QC procedures across the mine.

## AI/ML and digital twin

As more monitoring data are accumulated, data‑driven and hybrid AI/ML approaches are being  explored for anomaly detection, early warning, and residual capacity estimation of cementitious support [@ref-ml-shm; @ref-physics-informed]. Typical applications include detecting abnormal trends in strain or convergence relative to historical behaviour, or using multi‑sensor inputs to predict the probability of exceeding displacement or cracking limits. In parallel, digital twin concepts are being introduced, where numerical models of support and rock mass are continuously updated with sensing data to maintain a “live” representation of the underground excavations [@ref-digital-twin]. However, there are few mature applications for digital twins yet.

# Challenges and future rsearch directions

Although many sensing technologies have reached prototype or early commercial use in underground mines, several fundamental challenges still limit their widespread and reliable application to cementitious ground support systems [@ref-shm-review; @ref-mining-monitoring].

## Sensor longevity and robustness

At present, the first challenge is achieving sufficient robustness and service life for sensors embedded in shotcrete, backfill, and grouted bolts under harsh underground conditions.[@ref-underground-environment] Dust, moisture, aggressive groundwater, blasting vibration, and mechanical impact from equipment can degrade sensors, cables, and connectors, leading to drift or sudden failure.[@ref-corrosion-sensors] Traditional wired instruments add complexity in installation and maintenance, whereas wireless nodes face power‑supply and enclosure‑durability constraints in confined headings.[@ref-wireless-sensors] Future work should focus on mining‑specific packaging, low‑power designs, and self‑diagnostics to ensure that sensors remain reliable over representative fractions of the support lifecycle.[@ref-durability-sensing]

## Standardization QA/QC, and cost

A second challenge is the limited standardization of sensing practice for ground support in underground mining.[@ref-standards-shm] Existing regulations are mostly performance‑based and provide little technical guidance on sensor selection, calibration intervals, environmental qualification, redundancy, or data‑quality requirements.[@ref-guideline-groundsupport] Without common QA/QC frameworks, it is difficult to compare technologies, build trust, or evaluate cost‑effectiveness beyond initial purchase price.[@ref-cost-benefit] Future research and industry collaboration are needed to develop performance‑based guidelines that define minimum sensor suites, acceptance criteria, and documentation needs for different support types and risk levels.[@ref-risk-based-mining]

## Transition from monitoring to active control

A third challenge is turning heterogeneous monitoring data into reliable, predictive information about support condition and remaining capacity.[@ref-ml-shm; @ref-service-life] Datasets are often sparse, site‑specific, and biased toward normal operation, which complicates the training and validation of AI/ML models and digital twins.[@ref-digital-twin] There is still a weak link between measured indicators (e.g., DFOS strain, resistivity, half‑cell potential, AE activity) and quantitative performance metrics such as probability of cracking, debonding, or loss of load‑bearing capacity.[@ref-physics-informed] Future work should emphasize hybrid models that combine mechanics‑based understanding with data‑driven methods, as well as shared data formats and open interfaces that allow long‑term, multi‑site learning.[@ref-open-data]

Towards semi‑autonomous, risk‑informed control
Finally, there is a strategic challenge in moving from passive monitoring to risk‑informed, semi‑autonomous control of cementitious support.[@ref-shm-systems] In practice, sensing outputs are still rarely coupled to structured decision rules for re‑entry timing, support upgrade, or operational restrictions.[@ref-decision-framework] Research opportunities include simple, transparent decision trees that map sensing indicators to pre‑defined actions, and modular control architectures where orchestration platforms (e.g., OpenClaw) execute these actions under strict fail‑safe and human‑in‑the‑loop constraints.[@ref-openclaw] Addressing these challenges will be central to realizing the full future potential of sensing technologies for safer and more productive underground mining.[@ref-future-mining]

# Conclusion

This study establishes a lifecycle-oriented sensing framework that integrates physical variables, sensing technologies, and engineering decisions into a unified perspective. It demonstrates that no single sensing technology can satisfy all monitoring demands in underground mining environments. Instead, effective monitoring relies on the integration of complementary techniques, including embedded sensors, surface-attached instrumentation, external and remote sensing methods, and emerging self-sensing materials. Each modality provides distinct spatial and temporal resolution, and their combined use is essential for capturing multi-scale behavior under complex geological and operational conditions.

A key implication of this work is the need to move beyond isolated measurements toward system-level integration. The combination of multi-modal sensing, reliable data transmission, and data fusion enables the transformation of raw measurements into actionable information. In this context, sensing technologies play a central role in supporting critical decisions such as re-entry timing, support quality verification, maintenance planning, and hazard warning.

Future research should focus on improving sensor robustness under harsh underground conditions, developing standardized QA/QC frameworks, and advancing data integration methods. In particular, the coupling of sensing systems with IoT architectures, data-driven models, and digital twin concepts offers a pathway toward predictive and adaptive ground support management. Such developments will facilitate the transition from passive monitoring to risk-informed, autonomous control of cementitious support systems in underground mining.
